title: AI Gateway now runs canary ZDR audits
summary:
AI Gateway now runs canary audits against inference providers to detect when prompt content is read outside the inference path.

Contractual Zero Data Retention (ZDR) agreements and point-in-time security audits establish how a provider should handle your data, but production infrastructure changes continuously. Canary audits add a detection layer on top.

Each canary audit run:

  1. Mints unique URLs that exist nowhere else, each mapped privately to a specific provider, model, and audit run.

  2. Sends prompts containing those URLs through the normal inference path, with ZDR requested for covered providers and non-ZDR pairs included as positive controls.

title: Introducing Audited ZDR on AI Gateway
summary:
AI is now used in every part of a business, and as a result, companies send source code, customer records, and regulated data through inference providers.

The assurance that no data is retained after processing is still publicly unverified. Payment platforms, cloud infrastructure, and most other layers that handle data this sensitive have a way to prove their controls to outside parties, and inference will follow the same path.

Today we are introducing Audited ZDR on AI Gateway. A provider is labeled Audited ZDR only after an independent security firm tests its zero data retention claims against its code, infrastructure, and live traffic, then publishes the report. Baseten, Modal, and Wafer are launch partners that have already begun audits, and more providers are encouraged to join to help raise the bar for security and privacy.

title: A Practical Cheat Sheet for Exporting Short Video Clips for the Web
summary:
Short clips (10 to 90 seconds) end up everywhere: bug reports, docs, chat threads, landing pages. Most of the time people export them with whatever defaults their tool picks, and end up with either a 40 MB file for a 20-second clip or a blurry mess. Here is the cheat sheet I use.

1. Pick the resolution from the content

Content on screen Suggested height
Talking head, music, sports highlight 360p to 480p
UI walkthrough with normal-size text 720p
Code, terminal, dense dashboards 1080p (or crop to the region)

Chat apps (WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack previews) recompress uploads anyway, so for people-and-motion content 480p is usually indistinguishable after the app is done with it.

title: Convert a PDF to Markdown with MinerU from the command line
summary:
You have a PDF report and want it as Markdown: for your notes, or to give to an AI.

How do you do it?

You copy and paste from the PDF viewer. The headings turn into plain lines, and the tables turn into rows of numbers with no columns.

You ask an AI, and it points you to MinerU, which reads the layout and keeps headings and tables. You install it, start its server, and find the command:

mineru parse report.pdf --tier standard --pages 1-10 -o report.md --wait 600

Every flag matters. Leave out --pages and you only get the first 10 pages. Leave out --wait and a long document stops waiting after 60 seconds. --tier trades speed for quality.

summary:
Series 7 — Part 1 of 1

GraphQL in Flutter: Queries, Mutations, and Why It Changes How You Think About APIs

A standalone post on integrating GraphQL using the graphql_flutter package

Every API I had worked with in Flutter so far used REST — a fixed set of endpoints that return fixed data shapes. GraphQL is different. Instead of the server deciding what data you get, the client specifies exactly what it needs. I spent a day reading about GraphQL concepts and another day implementing a Flutter app that used it.

The GraphQL mental model

In REST you call GET /products and get everything the server thinks you need. In GraphQL you write a query that specifies exactly which fields you want:

summary:
This article was drafted with AI help and reviewed by the author.

Someone asks "how much will the WhatsApp AI assistant cost us a month?" and the first answer is usually the model bill.

That's one line out of three. When a Zap runs the flow, every AI reply also uses Zapier tasks, and the reply itself is a WhatsApp message that Meta may charge for. On a small or mid-sized flow the model line can end up the smallest of the three.

This post does two things. It gives you a per-reply formula you can fill in with your own numbers. Then it adds one Code by Zapier step that logs the real model cost of each reply on the HubSpot contact and flags a handoff when one conversation gets expensive.
